article.title: Growing Again
article.subtitle: Brad Jackson
article.linkLabel: Open article: Growing Again by Brad Jackson • 4 min read
article.description: I have wanted to post a note like this for more than a year, and finally, today, we have the results to make it possible.Growth is OxygenIn the fall o

posts.content:
In the life of every company, there are moments of joy and moments of challenge, moments of growth and moments of transition. Slalom has grown from a small 100-person company with big dreams in 2001 to a 13,000-team-member global services company.

Since our early days, I have mostly shared good news. Today is different. It is a day I thought would never come and one I hope will never occur again.

I just finished meeting with most of our team members to share the most difficult decision we have made in our history.

After extensively exploring and debating every option possible with our senior leaders, executive committee, and board of directors on how to best position our company during this time of significant shifts within our industry and to plan for the future, we have made the painful decision to restructure Slalom. This will result in approximately 7% of our team members leaving the company.

For a company like ours with such a deep commitment to the love of life and work, this is not easy to confront and even harder for those impacted.

It was important to me to have a clear set of principles guided by our core values for approaching reductions in our workforce.

- First and most importantly, do as much as possible for those affected.
- Second, consider the impact on customers in any decision.
- Third, reduce overlapping capabilities and internal initiatives that do not create customer value.
- And fourth, all reductions must be equitable and mapped to our future business strategy.

Over the coming days, we will focus on caring for our community and work to accompany each team member leaving with the utmost support as they move toward the next phase of their careers.
 
Today is the most challenging day in our company’s history as we share gratitude and say goodbye to some of our colleagues and friends. As we give ourselves time and grace to process this news, I appreciate any support you may offer to those leaving Slalom.

Change, though often difficult, can also be a catalyst for growth and transformation, and I look forward to sharing more in the coming weeks.

Dear Steve,
 
I remember the days when the mere thought of speaking in front of a crowd would leave me petrified with fear. Even the idea of presenting to a small group during an internal meeting made me uncomfortable. 
 
You pushed me out of my comfort zone and changed my life. You guided me with your grace, wisdom, and humor. You taught me that public speaking is about sharing a part of yourself. It's about connecting, engaging, and making an impact.
 
Your lessons will always echo in my heart, and your spirit and “world’s most wonderful smile” will continue to inspire me and everyone whose life you touched.
 
If the meaning of life is to leave this world better than you found it, you succeeded a million times over.
 
Rest in peace, my dear friend.
 
Brad

Question:
What does my 8-year-old daughter believe I do at work?

 
First, some context: 
Slalom Seattle recently hosted Bring Your Kids to Work Day. Our team members brought their children of all ages and I brought my young daughters. Kids practiced coding, they learned about their health from American Heart Association | American Stroke Association volunteers, and they explored the Seattle office, including meeting "the robot daddy." 

The day was innovative, unique, and well-received by the kids.  I was especially impressed when Hans Anderson (one of our leaders) took it one step further to help foster Slalom’s top priority: Customer Love. Hans brought Marissa, his 5-year-old daughter, to his client site where she delivered hand-crafted cards and lollipops to Hans' clients thanking them for the work they do. Marissa's imagination was sparked by her Dad’s work. 

Answer:
When I heard Hans' story, I was inspired to ask my daughter what she thinks I do at Slalom. Her response was, “You help people, Dad.” 

 
I encourage you to talk to your children about what you do at work; how we talk to and inspire our kids makes a difference for our next generation of leaders.

posts.content:
Can your work help change the world? At Slalom, we love solving our clients’ most challenging problems-  and for me the most exciting ones are projects that improve peoples’ lives.

 
Over the last quarter, 250+ Slalom employees have taken it to the next level by participating in a Hackathon for Social Good. Our last few hackathons have focused on machine learning and technologies like the HoloLens and Alexa, but this one involved all sixteen teams working on a digital product or process for a not-for-profit organization in their community.

 
All of the ideas and innovations were impactful – it was amazing to see the creativity and collaboration of the teams. The judges' favorite was a school safety mobile app that provides instant two-way messaging to assist in mitigating threats in schools. I believe that all the ideas that came out of the hack for social good will help level up the not-for-profits who partnered with our teams and thereby improve our communities.

 
I’ve realized that, like me, people also want to do more than donate and volunteer from time to time—they want to change the world. I challenge you to find ways to use your professional expertise to make the world a better place and to empower your teams to do the same.

posts.content:
“To live in hearts we leave behind is not to die.” – Thomas Campbell
 
Today in the United States it is Veterans Day, and across oceans and time zones it is Remembrance Day. The traditions vary, but the purpose is shared. We honor the people who served by leading, teaching, building, protecting, and strengthening the communities around them.
 
We pause.
We remember.
We say thank you.
 
Some of our teammates served. Others are still serving. Some have family and friends who did and do. Some carry memories that never fade. When you see them in meetings or on calls across the world, know that their service is not a story that ended when the uniform came off. It is part of who they are today.
 
If that is you, we see you. We honor you. We are grateful for you.
 
It has been said that we die twice. First when our life ends, and again the last time someone speaks our name. Remembrance is not only for those we have lost. It is also for the living. It is for the veterans standing beside us, carrying chapters they often did not ask for and experiences they cannot always talk about.
 
Not long ago, a veteran on the Slalom team shared something I have not forgotten. He said the hardest part of service was not the danger or the distance. It was coming home and wondering if anyone understood who he had become. He did not want praise. He just wanted to feel seen. That stayed with me, and it shaped this note.
 
Many veterans will tell you the most difficult part of service is not what happened while they wore the uniform. It is how invisible they felt when they took it off. When we listen with our full hearts, and when we acknowledge the path they walked, we are saying something veterans rarely hear. 

You belong.
You matter.
You are seen.

To every veteran around the world, thank you. Your courage allowed others to live with security, dignity, and possibility. You have given more than most will ever know, and we will not forget. You make us stronger!
 
Most of us will move through our routines today. But if you have a quiet moment, think of someone who served. Say their name out loud. Reach out to a veteran you know and thank them. A voice. A message. A moment of recognition. It might feel small to you. It might mean the world to them.
 
And in memorials around the world, people regularly place a hand on a name carved in stone. For a small moment, the past and present touch. Someone lived. Someone served. Someone mattered. Today, that truth continues. Service does not end with a date or a discharge. It lives on in steady hands, calm voices, quiet leadership, and the instinct to protect and lift others.
 
With deep admiration, gratitude, and respect.
